citation.sourceDocument: IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32 (2026 inflation adjustments, reflecting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act)
citation.sourceNote: The seven ordinary-income rates (10/12/22/24/32/35/37%) and their inflation-adjusted thresholds are transcribed from IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32, the annual inflation adjustments for taxable years beginning in 2026, reflecting the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Tables 1-4 of §2.01 give the per-status schedules and §2.14 gives the standard deduction: $32,200 married filing jointly and surviving spouse, $24,150 head of household, $16,100 single and married filing separately. Head of household is NOT a scaled version of single: its 12% and 22% bands open at $17,700 and $67,450 rather than $12,400 and $50,400, its 24% band shares single's $105,700, and then the two diverge again — 32% at $201,750 for head of household against $201,775 for single, and 35% at $256,200 against $256,225. Those last two are $25 apart, which is exactly the kind of near-identical pair that gets transcribed as a copy of its neighbour; each is checked against the Revenue Procedure's own '$X plus Y% of the excess' base amount, which reconciles only for the right threshold (head of household $39,207 = 16,155 + 24%·(201,750 − 105,700); single $41,024 = 17,966 + 24%·(201,775 − 105,700)). Omitted at launch fidelity, because the engine models a wage earner taking the standard deduction with no dependents: the additional standard deduction for age 65 or blindness ($1,650, or $2,050 if unmarried and not a surviving spouse), the capped dependent standard deduction, the §199A qualified business income deduction, the alternative minimum tax (which the AMT screener tile covers separately), and every credit. Itemized deductions are modeled separately by the take-home tile's 'big four'. Verified line by line against Rev. Proc. 2025-32 on 2026-08-29. The SALT limitation is statutory rather than indexed and comes from the Code, not this revenue procedure: IRC §164(b)(6)-(7), as rewritten by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, caps the state-and-local-tax itemized deduction at an applicable limitation amount of $40,400 for taxable years beginning in 2026 (§164(b)(7)(A)(ii)), reduced by 30% of modified adjusted gross income over $505,000 (§164(b)(7)(B)(i)-(ii)) but never below $10,000 (§164(b)(7)(B)(iii)), and halved for a married individual filing a separate return (§164(b)(6)(B)). The amount rises 1% a year through 2029 and reverts to $10,000 after, so 2027 is a transcription rather than a parse. IRC §170(p), added by the same Act (Pub. L. 119-21 §70424) for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, lets a filer who does not itemize deduct cash giving of up to $1,000 — $2,000 on a joint return — and §63(b)(4) subtracts it from adjusted gross income alongside the standard deduction rather than as part of it. It counts only cash contributions to §170(b)(1)(A) organizations, and not gifts to §509(a)(3) supporting organizations or donor-advised funds. IRC §151(d)(5)(C), from the same Act, allows $6,000 for each filer aged 65 or over — the taxpayer, and on a joint return the spouse — reduced by 6% of modified adjusted gross income over $75,000, or $150,000 on a joint return, and never below zero, so it runs out at $175,000 and $250,000. A married filer gets it only on a joint return (§151(d)(5)(C)(v)), and it applies whether or not the filer itemizes. It expires for taxable years beginning after 2028. IRC §224 and §225, from the same Act (§§70201, 70202), deduct qualified tips up to $25,000 and qualified overtime up to $12,500 — $25,000 on a joint return — each reduced by $100 for each $1,000 of modified adjusted gross income over $150,000, or $300,000 on a joint return. That phase-down counts WHOLE thousands: neither section says "or fraction thereof", unlike §24(b)(2). A married filer gets either only on a joint return (§224(f), §225(e)), and both terminate for taxable years beginning after 2028. IRC §163(h)(4), the Act's §70203 deduction for qualified passenger vehicle loan interest, is statutory too and read from the Code: up to $10,000 of interest for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024 and before January 1, 2029, reduced by $200 for each $1,000 (or portion thereof) of modified adjusted gross income over $100,000, or $200,000 on a joint return. Two readings that §§224 and 225 would get wrong: the "or portion thereof" in (C)(ii) makes a part-thousand count as a whole one, and the section carries no joint-return restriction, so a married individual filing separately is eligible at the single threshold. Verified against 26 U.S.C. §163(h)(4) and §63(b)(7) on 2026-09-01. IRC §170(b)(1)(I) is the other half of the Act's charitable rewrite and it runs the other way: "Any charitable contribution otherwise allowable ... shall be allowed only to the extent that the aggregate of such contributions exceeds 0.5 percent of the taxpayer's contribution base for the taxable year", added by §70425 for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. The contribution base is adjusted gross income computed without a net operating loss carryback (§170(b)(1)(H)), which for a wage earner is AGI. The floor applies before the percentage ceilings, not after. It does NOT reach the §170(p) deduction for a filer who does not itemize, and that is the statute's own instruction rather than an inference: §170(p) computes its figure "determined without regard to subsections (b)(1)(G)(ii), (b)(1)(I), and (d)(1)". So in 2026 the same $1,000 of giving is worth more to a non-itemizer than the first $1,000 is to an itemizer. Verified against 26 U.S.C. §170 on 2026-09-01. IRC §68 bites again in 2026 for the first time since 2017: the Act's §70111 rewrote it generally, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, and the old version had been switched off for every year from 2018 through 2025. It is no longer a phase-out of the deductions but a cap on their VALUE — itemized deductions "shall be reduced by 2/37 of the lesser of (1) such amount of itemized deductions, or (2) so much of the taxable income of the taxpayer for the taxable year (determined without regard to this section and increased by such amount of itemized deductions) as exceeds the dollar amount at which the 37 percent rate bracket under section 1 begins". Two thirty-sevenths of 37% is 2%, so a dollar of itemized deduction saves a top-bracket filer 35 cents rather than 37. The fraction is carried as the numerator and denominator the statute writes, since 2/37 does not terminate as a decimal; the threshold is not carried at all, because it is the start of this shard's own 37% bracket — $640,600 single and $768,700 joint for 2026 — and a second copy would be a second thing to drift. §68(b) applies it after every other limitation, which is where the engine puts it. Verified against 26 U.S.C. §68 on 2026-09-01. The §63(f) additional standard deduction for the aged is carried too, from the same procedure: "the additional standard deduction amount under §63(f) for the aged or the blind is $1,650. The additional standard deduction amount is increased to $2,050 if the individual is also unmarried and not a surviving spouse." It is per qualifying individual and it is an addition to the STANDARD deduction, so an itemizer does not get it — unlike §151(d)(5)(C)'s $6,000, which comes off either way and stacks on top of this. Only the aged half is modelled: this site does not ask whether a filer is blind, and §63(f)(2) grants the same amount again for blindness.
